summary: Describes a profile of the general MPLS loss, delay, and throughput measurement techniques from RFC 6374, tailored to MPLS Transport Profile networks. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a shorter, tailored version of a general measuring guide, picking the parts that fit one kind of network.

subtitle: A simplified profile of MPLS loss and delay measurement for MPLS transport networks.

tldr.problem: RFC 6374 defines general packet loss and delay measurement for MPLS, but transport network implementors need only a subset of it.
tldr.mechanism: This profile fixes default parameter values for externally configured sessions and lists the message intervals that should be supported, so negotiation is not needed.
tldr.outcome: Using the profile is purely optional, and it adds no new security considerations beyond RFC 6374.

today: RFC 6375 is an Informational document that has not been obsoleted or updated, and its profile remains optional.

sections.title: Purpose of the Profile
sections.content:
Procedures for measuring packet loss, delay and throughput in MPLS networks are defined in RFC 6374. RFC 6375 describes a profile, meaning a simplified subset of those procedures, that meets the requirements of MPLS-based transport networks (RFC 5921, RFC 5860).

Use of the profile is purely optional, and implementors may offer more of RFC 6374. It assumes devices are configured for measurement by external means, such as a Network Management System, and not by the measurement protocols themselves. It comes from a joint IETF and ITU-T effort on an MPLS Transport Profile.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a short version of a big guide, for people who only run one kind of network. You do not have to use it.

sections.title: What Carries Over from RFC 6374
sections.content: The measurement considerations of Section 2.9 of RFC 6374 apply to MPLS-TP too, except two that concern topologies MPLS-TP excludes. These are Equal Cost Multipath, and direct Loss Measurement with Label Switched Paths built by the Label Distribution Protocol or using Penultimate Hop Popping.
sections.plainLanguage: Most of the old advice still applies. Two bits are skipped because this kind of network never does those things.

sections.title: Loss Measurement Defaults
sections.content:
When a Loss Measurement (LM) session is configured externally, the endpoints can fix parameters in advance so none are negotiated. The defaults are: query control code In-band Response Requested, Byte/packet Count (B) flag set to packet count, Traffic-class-specific (T) flag set to traffic-class-scoped, and Origin Timestamp Format Truncated IEEE 1588v2.

Simple implementations may assume both ends use these defaults, but are strongly advised to validate received values to detect configuration inconsistencies. Operators should be able to set rates per channel. LM messages should support intervals of 100 milliseconds, 1 second, 10 seconds, 1 minute and 10 minutes. Test messages (used for inferred LM) should support 10 milliseconds, 100 milliseconds, 1 second, 10 seconds and 1 minute.
sections.plainLanguage: Both ends agree on the settings ahead of time, so they never need to chat about them. They still double-check each message.

sections.title: Delay Measurement Defaults and Security
sections.content:
For Delay Measurement (DM), the defaults are the same In-band Response Requested query control code, and Truncated IEEE 1588v2 for the Querier Timestamp Format, the Responder Timestamp Format and the Responder's Preferred Timestamp Format. The same advice to validate received values applies. DM messages should be configurable per channel with intervals of 1 second, 10 seconds, 1 minute and 10 minutes.

The profile introduces no new security considerations, and those of RFC 6374 apply, along with the MPLS-TP security framework.
sections.plainLanguage: Timing checks use the same kind of pre-agreed settings. They can be sent every second, or less often.
